title: Welcome to the Messy Middle
summary: Explore a different perspective with Nathan Macintosh and Camille Stewart Gloster, one that challenges some of the biggest assumptions surrounding AI today.
body_markdown:
It’s easy to talk about AI as if the future has already been written. AI will transform work. AI will replace jobs. AI will reshape industries. The assumption is that the technology is simply moving forward, and the rest of us are along for the ride. But what if


[the future of AI](https://www.commvault.com/resources/whitepaper/resops-and-the-future-of-resilient-business-in-the-era-of-ai) isn’t as predetermined as it seems?


In this episode of


*Ready. Or Not.* (S2:E3), Nathan Macintosh sits down with cybersecurity and AI strategist Camille Stewart Gloster, whose experience spans the White House, the Department of Homeland Security, Google, and national cybersecurity policy. Together, they explore a different perspective, one that challenges some of the biggest assumptions surrounding AI today.


[Watch the full episode on Readiverse .](https://www.readiverse.com/resources/video/welcome-to-the-messy-middle-with-camille-gloster)


#### Key Takeaways


- Organizations have more influence over the future of AI than they may realize.


- AI is advancing rapidly, but organizations still have a say in how it’s deployed, governed, and trusted.


- Security is not separate from an AI strategy. It’s what helps make AI reliable, governable, and effective.


- [AI agents](https://www.commvault.com/blogs/ai-protect-ai-agents-are-everywhere-do-you-know-what-theyre-doing) should be managed more like digital employees than software tools.


- Many organizations are struggling to see meaningful results from AI because they’re adding it to existing processes instead of redesigning them.


#### Reframing the Conversation Around AI


Camille argues that while AI technologies will continue to advance, the outcomes they create are far from predetermined. The choices organizations make about


[governance, security, and accountability](https://www.commvault.com/en-ae/blogs/how-can-organizations-achieve-resilience-in-the-ai-era) will help shape what comes next.


As Nathan notes early in the conversation:


> **“You’re the only person so far in this whole series that has used the phrase ‘AI** **is not inevitable.’”**
> *– Nathan Macintosh*


It’s a simple observation, but it reframes the discussion about the future of AI. Instead of asking what AI will do to us, Camille asks what role we want to play in shaping what comes next.


####


Your Decisions Matter


At the heart of this conversation is Camille’s belief that


AI is not inevitable. Her point isn’t that AI technologies might disappear. In fact, many AI capabilities are already embedded in the software and services we use every day.


What isn’t inevitable, she argues, are the assumptions we’ve already started drawing about the future.


> **“You have a lot more control than you realize.”**
> *– Camille Stewart Gloster*


Discussions about AI often focus on what the technology can do, while paying far less attention to the choices people, organizations, and governments can make. For security and technology leaders, that means shifting the conversation from prediction to responsibility. Instead of wondering what AI will become, organizations should be focused on the systems they’re building, what risks they’re introducing, and who will be accountable when something goes wrong.


Camille’s perspective is a reminder that the most important AI decisions may have less to do with algorithms and more to do with the people responsible for putting them into practice.


####


Security Makes AI Possible


Camille points out that security and AI strategy are deeply connected. Not just in the traditional sense of protecting systems from hackers or preventing data leaks, but in understanding how agents behave, what information they’re using, and what actions they’re allowed to take.


Deploying AI isn’t just about adding a new capability. It’s about understanding how that capability changes the organization’s risk profile.


> **“Any organization thinking about how to maximize their investment in AI needs to invest in their security team.”**
>
>
> *– Camille Stewart Gloster*


As Camille explains, organizations are introducing new actors into their environments, and they should think about these AI agents more like employees than software. When a company hires a person, it defines responsibilities, establishes oversight, and creates accountability measures. The same should apply to AI agents.


Throughout the conversation, Camille doesn’t frame security as something that slows innovation down. Instead, she sees it as what makes innovation sustainable. As agents take on more responsibility, organizations need a way to understand and govern them. In that sense, security isn’t just about reducing risk. It’s what gives organizations the confidence to adopt AI at scale.


#### Sneak Peek: The New Security Mindset


Camille wants to broaden the scope of security beyond preventing breaches. In this clip, she explains why controlling and understanding AI systems is just as important as deploying them in the first place.


#### AI Is Not a Quick Fix


Many organizations are investing heavily in AI, but that investment doesn’t automatically translate into results. According to Camille, one reason is that companies often layer new technology onto old ways of working instead of taking a more thoughtful approach.


> **“The best way to get value out of investing in AI is probably to redesign a** **process.”**
> *– Camille Stewart Gloster*


Camille emphasizes that AI is most effective when it’s part of a broader transformation effort. Rather than looking for opportunities to insert AI into individual tasks, organizations should examine how work flows and identify where the process itself can be redesigned and improved.


She also notes that organizations frequently underestimate the work required to successfully adopt AI. Real value comes not only from the technology itself, but from the operational changes that support it.


Perhaps the biggest lesson is that AI is rarely the entire answer. The real opportunity comes from pairing new technology with thoughtful changes to processes and workflows, so AI can become part of something larger than AI itself. than AI itself.


#### Ready for Some Optimism?


AI conversations often swing between extremes. Either AI is going to solve everything, or it’s going to completely upend the way we live and work. Camille offers a positive perspective.


Throughout the episode, she emphasizes that organizations have more influence over the future of AI than they may realize. AI’s future will be shaped by the decisions organizations make about security, governance, accountability, and trust. AI’s future will be shaped by the decisions organizations make about security, governance, accountability, and trust.


That also aligns with a recurring theme of


*Ready. Or Not.* Staying ready isn’t about predicting the future. It’s about making thoughtful decisions that help you navigate it.


AI will keep advancing, and new opportunities and risks will emerge. But as Camille reminds us, organizations have more influence over what comes next than they sometimes realize. And that’s a much more empowering way to think about the future of AI.


---


##### FAQs


**Q: What does Camille mean when she says “AI is not inevitable”?**


**A:** Camille’s point is that while AI technologies will continue to advance, the social, economic, and organizational outcomes associated with AI are not predetermined. Leaders, policymakers, and businesses still have significant influence over how AI is deployed, governed, and regulated. The future is being shaped by human decisions, not technology alone.


**Q: Why does Camille compare AI agents to employees?**


**A:** AI agents increasingly take actions, access systems, process information, and make decisions on behalf of organizations. Because of that, they require many of the same guardrails businesses apply to human workers, including role definition, oversight, permissions management, accountability, and continuous monitoring.


**Q: Why does security become more important as AI adoption increases?**


**A:** As AI systems gain access to data, applications, and business processes, organizations need ways to control and monitor their behavior. Security teams help establish governance, implement safeguards, create visibility into agent activity, and verify AI systems operate within defined boundaries. Without those controls, the risks associated with autonomous systems can increase significantly.


**Q: Why aren’t some organizations seeing meaningful results from AI?**


**A:** According to Camille, many businesses are simply layering AI onto existing processes rather than redesigning workflows around new capabilities. Real value often comes from rethinking how work is performed, identifying opportunities to scale successful AI-driven practices, and investing in the operational changes needed to support long-term adoption.


**Q: What are runtime guardrails, and why do they matter?**


**A:** Runtime guardrails are controls that allow organizations to monitor and evaluate agent behavior while actions are taking place. Rather than relying solely on static rules, these guardrails provide opportunities to review decisions, intervene when necessary, and escalate actions to humans before problems occur. They help organizations balance autonomy with accountability.


**Q: What’s the biggest lesson from this episode?**


**A:** AI strategy and security strategy can no longer be treated as separate conversations. The organizations that succeed with AI are often the ones that combine innovation with governance, empowering agents to create value while making sure that humans remain responsible for the outcomes. That’s not just how you reduce risk. It’s how you build trust in the technology itself.’s how you build trust in the technology itself.
